hook: He wrote more mathematics than anyone who ever lived, and much of it after he went blind.

pages.x: Leonhard Euler was born in Basel, Switzerland, in 1707. His father, a pastor, hoped he would be one too. He went to the university at 13, where Johann Bernoulli, one of the best mathematicians in Europe, saw his gift, gave him lessons on Saturday afternoons and talked his father into letting him study mathematics instead.

In 1727, aged 20, he took a post at the Academy of Sciences that Peter the Great had founded in St Petersburg. He was hired for physiology but was soon doing mathematics, and at 26 he was put in charge of it. In 1734 he married Katharina Gsell, the daughter of a Swiss painter; of their 13 children, only five grew up.

For 85 years the best mathematicians, the Bernoullis of Basel among them, had tried to find the exact total of 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 and so on forever, one over every square number. In 1735 Euler found it: π²/6, about 1.645. Nobody had expected π, the number of circles, to turn up. It made him famous across Europe.

People in Königsberg wondered if they could walk through their city crossing each of its seven bridges exactly once. In 1736 Euler proved they could not, and showed why: all that counts is how many bridges meet each piece of land.
pages.fx: It was the first problem of graph theory, the mathematics of networks, which today plans delivery routes, maps the internet and finds the way on a phone.

pages.x: In 1738, after a fever, he lost the sight of his right eye. "Now I will have fewer distractions," he is said to have joked. In 1741, with Russia in turmoil, he moved to the Academy of Frederick the Great in Berlin and stayed 25 years. The king, who loved clever talk, found the plain, devout Euler dull, and nicknamed him the Cyclops.
pages.cap: Frederick the Great, his new master

pages.x: In 1748 he showed that e^ix = cos x + i sin x, joining the number e of growth, the circles of trigonometry and i, the "imaginary" square root of −1. Put in π for x and it becomes e^iπ + 1 = 0: five key numbers in one line.
pages.fx: It is often called the most beautiful equation in mathematics, and it is everyday work for engineers, who use it to calculate alternating current, radio waves and sound.

pages.x: Frederick wanted fountains for his palace at Sanssouci, and Euler worked out the pumps. The water never rose, and years later the king mocked him in a letter: "Vanity of vanities! Vanity of geometry!" Historians who have checked think Euler's sums were probably right, and the fault lay with the work as it was built.

In 1766 Catherine the Great invited him back to St Petersburg, and soon a cataract took the sight of his other eye. When fire swept through his house in 1771, a craftsman from Basel carried him out. Yet he worked on, doing long sums in his head and dictating to his sons and helpers: in 1775 he finished about a paper a week.
pages.cap: Catherine the Great, who brought him back

pages.x: On 18 September 1783 he gave a grandson a mathematics lesson, worked out with chalk how the new hot-air balloons rise, and talked about Uranus, the planet found two years before. That afternoon he had a stroke, and he died a few hours later. In the words of the French mathematician Condorcet, he "ceased to calculate and to live".
pages.cap: Uranus, the new planet he talked about that day

pages.x: Euler wrote more mathematics than anyone else in history: over 800 books and papers. Formulas and theorems named after him run through every part of mathematics. Laplace is said to have told his students: "Read Euler, read Euler, he is the master of us all."

Founded graph theory with the bridges of Königsberg
